state.case_summary:
A 53-year-old white male presented to the emergency room with acute central chest pain lasting 8 hours. The pain occurred mainly at rest, was non-radiating, and was not accompanied by sweating, palpitations, nausea, or vomiting. He experienced three similar episodes in the previous week. He reported no changes in bowel habits or other gastrointestinal symptoms. His medical history included hypertension diagnosed 6 months prior, for which he was prescribed Bendrofluazide, though he admitted to non-compliance. He smoked 20 cigarettes per day and consumed 6–8 units of alcohol daily. His family history included his father and five paternal uncles who died from ischemic heart disease in their early fifties, and his mother who died at 57 from cervical carcinoma. He has one living sister. He was able to walk up to 5 miles a day without chest discomfort before this admission. On examination, he had a heart rate of 103 beats per minute in sinus rhythm, blood pressure of 167/129 mmHg, oxygen saturation of 97% on room air, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, and a normal temperature of 36.7°C. His BMI was 27.6. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Fundoscopic examination showed lipaemia retinalis. A 12-lead ECG on admission showed no ischemic changes except for peaked T waves. Chest X-ray was normal. Troponin T levels could not be measured on three occasions due to lipaemia, but CK-MB was normal at 3 μg/l. An exercise tolerance test conducted the next morning was negative for reversible ischemic changes.

Admission lipid profile revealed a markedly raised TG at 103 mmol/l. Next morning repeats lipid profile; TG and total cholesterol (Tchol) were 57 mmol/l and 32 mmol/l, respectively. HDL cholesterol was unmeasurable with urea 4.5 mmol/l, creatinine 86 μmol/l, total protein 67 g/l, albumin 39 g/l and urine albumin/creatinine ratio 9.7. Fasting glucose and HBA1c were normal at 4.5 mmol/l and 5.8%, respectively. Liver function test revealed a moderately raised ALT and GGT at 60 U/l and 730 U/l, respectively. Serum amylase was normal at 51 U/l.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
